idiom_name: top-level extension functions (compiled to static methods)
implementation_notes: Kotlin's extension functions are the language's servant facility: a top-level fun Circle.moveTo(to: Position) adds the behaviour to a type you do not own, is called with member syntax, and compiles to a static method whose first parameter is the receiver (Java sees MoveKt.moveTo(circle, to)). The capability interface is expressed as the receiver type or a generic bound - fun <T : Movable> List<T>.moveAllTo(...) - and dispatch is static, so extensions are resolved at compile time and can never be overridden. Keep the classic servant object when the behaviour carries policy state, when it must be substituted in tests, or when it should not appear on the serviced type at every call site.
pitfalls: Extensions are resolved statically and never override: a member of the same signature (present now, or added later by a library upgrade) silently wins, and an extension cannot be mocked - tests need a real receiver or a servant object.
An extension cannot reach private or protected members, so a servant that needs the representation must be a member or an internal helper; do not widen visibility just to let the extension in.
Same-named extensions from different packages both compile and the import decides which one runs - a trap when two libraries extend the same type.
sources: Kotlin documentation, Extensions - extension functions/properties 'extend a class or an interface with new functionality without using inheritance or design patterns like Decorator', call-as-member syntax and static resolution; https://kotlinlang.org/docs/extensions.html
